metadata.file_name: 7. Alas & Tezer. (2024). Artificial Neural Network and Adaptive Neuro Fuzzy Inference System Hybridized Models in the Sustainable Integration of Language and Mathematics Skills: The Case of Singapore and Hong Kong.pdf
metadata.title: Artificial Neural Network and Adaptive Neuro Fuzzy Inference System Hybridized Models in the Sustainable Integration of Language and Mathematics Skills: The Case of Singaporeand Hong Kong

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 as an external reference for mathematics and reading outcomes, but the empirical modeling is performed on curriculum content-analysis outputs (counts/frequencies of language-skill themes in mathematics curricula) mapped to PISA scores for Singapore and Hong Kong. The manuscript describes document/content analysis and then trains ANN (MLP) and ANFIS models in MATLAB using a simple train/test/validation split (70%/15%/15%). No PISA microdata sampling design, complex survey design, or any student/sampling weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) are mentioned, and the modeling is not framed as a weighted survey analysis. Given the ML setup and the absence of any explicit weighting discussion, the analysis is treated as unweighted; replicate-weight methods (BRR/jackknife) are not reported.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variable used in the ANN/ANFIS models is based on PISA scores at the country level (Singapore and Hong Kong) and on curriculum content-analysis frequencies, rather than on student-level cognitive achievement PVs. The paper does not describe any missing-data strategy for the curriculum-derived inputs or the PISA-score targets, which is a reporting gap because the modeling pipeline (ANN/ANFIS) requires complete numeric inputs for training and evaluation.
data.outcome_summary: The study compares two ML models (ANN/MLP and ANFIS) linking curriculum-derived language-skill indicators to PISA-based language skills for Singapore and Hong Kong. For the ANN model (Model 1), performance is RMSE = 17.6385 and R² = 0.353954, indicating an insufficient relationship between verbal skills and language skills based on PISA scores. For the ANFIS model (Model 2), performance improves slightly with RMSE = 12.42771 and R² = 0.397867, but the relationship is still judged insufficient. Across both models, the authors conclude that the language–mathematics relationship is not explained purely by curriculum/program content. The manuscript does not report any survey-weighted or PV-based student-level modeling; it uses curriculum content analysis and country-level PISA score comparisons.
